lead: Paul’s first recorded sermon is preached in a synagogue, after the reading of the Law and the Prophets. He tells Israel’s story from Egypt to David and then names its fulfilment: “Of this man’s posterity God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised.” In the Gospel, just after the washing of the feet, Jesus tells the Twelve that whoever receives the one he sends receives him. Psalm 89 sings of God’s covenant with David, the thread that ties both readings together.

set: From Cyprus the missionaries sail to the south coast of Asia Minor and go inland to Antioch in Pisidia, a Roman colony, not to be confused with Antioch in Syria. Luke now calls Saul by his Roman name, Paul (13:9), and Paul takes the lead. John Mark goes back to Jerusalem; Luke gives no reason, but the departure will later divide Paul and Barnabas (15:37–39). The order of the synagogue service matches what we know from other sources: readings from the Law and the Prophets, then a word of teaching (compare Luke 4:16–21).
str: vv. 13–15: the journey to Antioch in Pisidia; the invitation after the readings.
vv. 16–22: God’s deeds from the exodus to David.
vv. 23–25: from David to Jesus, with John the Baptist as witness.
kw: The same phrase describes the Letter to the Hebrews (Hebrews 13:22). It seems to have been a name for a sermon after the readings, as the homily follows the readings at Mass.

Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel and attended the synagogue without becoming full converts, like Cornelius (10:2). Paul addresses them together with the Israelites (v. 16): the bridge by which the Gospel would reach the nations was already standing.
God has brought Israel “a Savior”, the title the angel gave at Bethlehem (Luke 2:11). Paul presents Jesus not as a break with Israel’s story but as its promised goal.
vv: I have found David, son of Jesse, to be a man after my heart, who will carry out all my wishes.

A weaving together of Scripture: Psalm 89:20 (“I have found my servant David”), 1 Samuel 13:14 (“a man after his own heart”) and Isaiah 44:28 (“he shall carry out all my purpose”). Paul preaches as a Jew formed by the Scriptures.
Of this man’s posterity God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised;
The center of the sermon. God keeps a promise across a thousand years.
I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet.
Untying sandals was a slave’s task. The last and greatest of the prophets places himself below even that service.
ch: The Church sees in Paul’s sermon a model of how the Old Testament is read in the light of Christ: Israel’s history is not set aside but fulfilled. The Second Vatican Council, following St Augustine, says that the New Testament is hidden in the Old and the Old is made manifest in the New (Dei Verbum 16). At Mass the homily stands where Paul’s “word of exhortation” stood: after the readings, opening them for today.

r.h: Whoever receives one whom I send
set: Jesus has just washed the feet of his disciples (13:1–15) and told them to do the same for one another. These verses draw out the meaning: the servant is not above the master, and blessing lies not in knowing but in doing. In the same breath Jesus speaks of the betrayer, and yet he ends with the dignity of those he sends.
str: vv. 16–17: servant and master; the blessing of doing.
v. 18: “The one who ate my bread”: Psalm 41.
v. 19: foretold so that they may believe “I am he”.
kw: The word in v. 16 translated “messengers” is apostolos, the only place it occurs in John’s Gospel. The Twelve hear their name and their place at the same moment: sent ones, no greater than the one who sends them.

Literally “I am”. In Isaiah God says “I am he” to show that he alone foretells and fulfils (Isaiah 43:10). Jesus speaks so that his Passion, when it comes, will reveal who he is rather than disprove it.
As in the Beatitudes. John has only two such beatitudes (13:17; 20:29). Here the blessing belongs not to knowing the example but to doing it.
vv: you are blessed if you do them.
Knowing about service is easy; the blessing is promised to those who wash feet.
The one who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.

From Psalm 41:9, the prayer of a man betrayed by a trusted friend. To eat someone’s bread was to be bound in friendship; lifting the heel pictures a kick, or turning one’s back. The betrayal comes from within the circle of the table.
whoever receives one whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.

A chain runs from the Father to the humblest messenger of the Gospel. Jewish teaching knew a similar principle about envoys, later written in the Mishnah: a man’s agent is like the man himself (Berakhot 5:5).
ch: The Church hears in v. 20 a foundation of apostolic ministry: Christ sends the apostles as the Father sent him (20:21), and whoever receives them receives him (CCC 858). The dignity of the minister is not his own; it is Christ’s, and so it calls first for humility, since the servant is not greater than the master. The betrayer at the table reminds the Church that even those closest to Christ must keep watch over their hearts.

study: Paul read Israel’s history as leading to Jesus. Can I tell the story of my own life in the same way, seeing where God kept his promises?
Whom has Christ sent into my life this week? How did I receive them?
